{{Short description|Equation in thermodynamics}}
[[File:Josiah_Willard_Gibbs_-from_MMS-.jpg | thumb | 220x124px | right | alt= Josiah Willard Gibbs | Josiah Willard Gibbs]]
In [[thermodynamics]], the '''Gibbs–Duhem equation''' describes the relationship between changes in [[chemical potential]] for components in a [[thermodynamic system]]:<ref>{{cite book | last = Perrot | first = Pierre | title = A to Z of Thermodynamics | date = 1998 | publisher = Oxford University Press | isbn = 978-0-19-856556-7 | location = Oxford}}</ref>

<math display="block">\sum_{i=1}^I N_i \mathrm{d}\mu_i = - S \mathrm{d}T + V \mathrm{d}p</math>

where <math>N_i</math> is the number of [[mole (unit)|moles]] of component <math>i, \mathrm{d}\mu_i </math> the [[infinitesimal]] increase in chemical potential for this component, <math>S</math> the [[entropy]], <math>T</math> the [[absolute temperature]], <math>V</math> [[volume]] and <math>p</math> the [[pressure]]. <math>I</math> is the number of different components in the system. This equation shows that in thermodynamics [[intensive property|intensive properties]] are not independent but related, making it a mathematical statement of the [[state postulate]]. When pressure and temperature are variable, only <math>I-1 </math> of <math>I</math> components have independent values for chemical potential and [[Gibbs' phase rule]] follows.

The Gibbs−Duhem equation applies to homogeneous thermodynamic systems. It does not apply to inhomogeneous systems such as small thermodynamic systems,<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Stephenson | first1 = J. | title = Fluctuations in Particle Number in a Grand Canonical Ensemble of Small Systems | doi = 10.1119/1.1987755 | journal = American Journal of Physics | volume = 42 | issue = 6 | pages = 478–481 | year = 1974 }}</ref> systems subject to long-range forces like electricity and gravity,<ref name="sorensen">{{Cite journal |last=Sørensen |first=Torben Smith |last2=Compañ |first2=Vicente |date=1997 |title=On the Gibbs-Duhem equation for thermodynamic systems of mixed Euler order with special reference to gravitational and nonelectroneutral systems |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0013468696002095 |journal=Electrochimica Acta |language=en |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=639–649 |doi=10.1016/S0013-4686(96)00209-5|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dunning-Davies |first=J. |date=1983 |title=Extensivity and the Gibbs-Duhem equation |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0375960183906539 |journal=Physics Letters A |language=en |volume=97 |issue=8 |pages=327–328 |doi=10.1016/0375-9601(83)90653-9|url-access=subscription }}</ref> or to fluids in porous media.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brochard |first=Laurent |last2=Honório |first2=Túlio |date=2020 |title=Revisiting thermo-poro-mechanics under adsorption: Formulation without assuming Gibbs-Duhem equation |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0020722520300847 |journal=International Journal of Engineering Science |language=en |volume=152 |article-number=103296 |doi=10.1016/j.ijengsci.2020.103296}}</ref>

The equation is named after [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]] and [[Pierre Duhem]].<!-- need cite for original paper, so could give timeframe of its publication -->

==Derivation==

The Gibbs–Duhem equation follows from assuming the system can be scaled in amount perfectly. Gibbs derived the relationship based on the [[thought experiment]] of varying the [[amount of substance]] starting from zero, keeping its nature and state the same.<ref name="sorensen"/>

Mathematically, this means the internal energy <math>U</math> scales with its extensive variables as follows:<ref name="callen">{{cite book | first = Herbert B. | last = Callen | author-link = Herbert Callen | year = 1985 | title = Thermodynamics and an Introduction to Thermostatistics | edition = 2nd | publisher = John Wiley & Sons | location = New York | isbn = 978-0-471-86256-7 | pages=61-62 }}</ref>
<math display="block">U(\lambda S, \lambda V, \lambda N_1, \lambda N_2, \ldots) = \lambda U (S, V, N_1, N_2, \ldots)</math>
where <math>S, V, N_1, N_2, \ldots</math> are all of the extensive variables of system: entropy, volume, and particle numbers. The [[internal energy]] is thus a [[Homogeneous function|first-order homogenous function]]. Applying [[Homogeneous function#Positive homogeneity|Euler's homogeneous function theorem]], one finds the following relation:

<math display="block">U = TS - pV + \sum_{i=1}^I \mu_i N_i</math>

Taking the total differential, one finds

<math display="block">\mathrm{d}U = T\mathrm{d}S + S\mathrm{d}T - p\mathrm{d}V - V \mathrm{d}p + \sum_{i=1}^I \mu_i \mathrm{d} N_i + \sum_{i=1}^I N_i \mathrm{d} \mu_i </math>

From both sides one can subtract the [[fundamental thermodynamic relation]],
<math display="block">\mathrm{d}U = T\mathrm{d}S - p\mathrm{d}V + \sum_{i=1}^I \mu_i \mathrm{d} N_i </math>

yielding the Gibbs–Duhem equation<ref name="callen"/>

<math display="block">0 =S\mathrm{d}T - V \mathrm{d}p + \sum_{i=1}^I N_i \mathrm{d} \mu_i .</math>

==Applications==
By normalizing the above equation by the extent of a system, such as the total number of moles, the Gibbs–Duhem equation provides a relationship between the intensive variables of the system. For a simple system with <math>I</math> different components, there will be <math>I+1 </math> independent parameters or "degrees of freedom". For example, if we know a gas cylinder filled with pure nitrogen is at room temperature (298&nbsp;K) and 25&nbsp;MPa, we can determine the fluid density (258&nbsp;kg/m<sup>3</sup>), enthalpy (272&nbsp;kJ/kg), entropy (5.07&nbsp;kJ/kg⋅K) or any other intensive thermodynamic variable.<ref>Calculated using [[REFPROP]]: NIST Standard Reference Database 23, Version 8.0</ref> If instead the cylinder contains a nitrogen/oxygen mixture, we require an additional piece of information, usually the ratio of oxygen-to-nitrogen.

If multiple phases of matter are present, the chemical potentials across a phase boundary are equal.<ref>''Fundamentals of Engineering Thermodynamics, 3rd Edition'' Michael J. Moran and Howard N. Shapiro, p. 710 {{ISBN|0-471-07681-3}}</ref> Combining expressions for the Gibbs–Duhem equation in each phase and assuming systematic equilibrium (i.e. that the temperature and pressure is constant throughout the system), we recover the [[Gibbs' phase rule]].

One particularly useful expression arises when considering binary solutions.<ref>''The Properties of Gases and Liquids, 5th Edition'' Poling, Prausnitz and O'Connell, p. 8.13, {{ISBN|0-07-011682-2}}</ref> At constant P ([[Isobaric process|isobaric]]) and T ([[isothermal]]) it becomes:

<math display="block">0= N_1 \mathrm{d}\mu_1 + N_2 \mathrm{d}\mu_2 </math>

or, normalizing by total number of moles in the system <math>N_1 + N_2,</math> substituting in the definition of [[activity coefficient]] <math> \gamma</math> and using the identity <math> x_1 + x_2 = 1 </math>:<ref>{{ cite book | last = Stølen | first = Svein | title = Chemical Thermodynamics of Materials: Macroscopic and Microscopic Aspects | last2 = Grande | first2 = Tor | last3 = Allan | first3 = Neil L. | date = 2008 | publisher = Wiley |isbn = 978-0-471-49230-6 | edition = Transferred to digital print |location = Chichester | page = 79}}</ref>

<math display="block">0 = x_1 \mathrm{d}\ln(\gamma_1) + x_2 \mathrm{d}\ln(\gamma_2)</math>

This equation is instrumental in the calculation of thermodynamically consistent and thus more accurate expressions for the [[vapor pressure]] of a binary mixture from limited experimental data. One can develop this further to the [[Duhem–Margules equation]] which relates to vapor pressures directly.

== Ternary and multicomponent solutions and mixtures==

[[Lawrence Stamper Darken]] has shown that the Gibbs–Duhem equation can be applied to the determination of chemical potentials of components from a multicomponent system from experimental data regarding the chemical potential <math>\bar {G_2}</math> of only one component (here component 2) at all compositions. He has deduced the following relation<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Darken | first1 = L. S | title = Application of the Gibbs-Duhem Equation to Ternary and Multicomponent Systems | doi = 10.1021/ja01163a030 | journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume = 72 | issue = 7 | pages = 2909–2914 | year = 1950 }}</ref>

<math display="block">\bar{G_2} = G + (1-x_2) \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial x_2}\right)_{\frac{x_1}{x_3}}</math>

x<sub>i</sub>, amount (mole) fractions of components.

Making some rearrangements and dividing by (1 – x<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup> gives:

<math display="block">\frac{G}{(1-x_2)^2} + \frac{1}{1-x_2} \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial x_2}\right)_{\frac{x_1}{x_3}} = \frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1-x_2)^2}</math>

or

<math display="block"> \left(\mathfrak{d} \frac{G}{\frac{1 - x_2}{\mathfrak{d} x_2}}\right)_{\frac{x_1}{x_3}} = \frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2}</math>

or 

<math display="block">\left(\frac {\frac{\partial G}{1-x_2}}{\partial x_2}\right)_{\frac{x_1}{x_3}} = \frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2}</math> as formatting variant

The derivative with respect to one [[mole fraction]] x<sub>2</sub> is taken at constant ratios of amounts (and therefore of mole fractions) of the other components of the solution representable in a diagram like [[ternary plot]].

The last equality can be integrated from <math>x_2 = 1</math> to <math>x_2</math> gives:

<math display="block">G - (1 - x_2) \lim_{x_2\to 1} \frac{G}{1 - x_2} = (1 - x_2) \int_{1}^{x_2}\frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2} dx_2 </math>

Applying [[l'Hôpital's rule]] gives:

<math display="block"> \lim_{x_2\to 1} \frac{G}{1 - x_2} = \lim_{x_2\to 1} \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial x_2}\right)_{\frac{x_1}{x_3}} .</math>

This becomes further:

<math display="block"> \lim_{x_2\to 1} \frac{G}{1 - x_2} = -\lim_{x_2\to 1} \frac {\bar{G_2} - G}{1 - x_2}.</math>

Express the mole fractions of component 1 and 3 as functions of component 2 mole fraction and binary mole ratios:

<math display="block">x_1 = \frac{1-x_2}{1+\frac{x_3}{x_1}}</math>
<math display="block">x_3 = \frac{1-x_2}{1+\frac{x_1}{x_3}}</math>

and the sum of partial molar quantities

<math display="block">G=\sum _{i=1}^3 x_i \bar{G_i},</math>

gives 

<math display="block">G= x_1 (\bar {G_1})_{x_2 =1} + x_3 (\bar {G_3})_{x_2 =1} + (1 - x_2) \int_{1}^{x_2}\frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2} dx_2 </math>

<math>(\bar{G_1})_{x_2 =1}</math> and <math>(\bar{G_3})_{x_2 =1}</math> are constants which can be determined from the binary systems 1_2 and 2_3. These constants can be obtained from the previous equality by putting the complementary mole fraction x<sub>3</sub> = 0 for x<sub>1</sub> and vice versa.

Thus 

<math display="block">(\bar {G_1})_{x_2 =1} = - \left(\int_{1}^{0}\frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2} dx_2 \right)_{x_3=0}</math>

and 

<math display="block">(\bar {G_3})_{x_2 =1} = - \left(\int_{1}^{0}\frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2} dx_2 \right)_{x_1=0}</math>

The final expression is given by substitution of these constants into the previous equation:

<math display="block">G= (1 - x_2) \left(\int_{1}^{x_2}\frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2} dx_2 \right)_{\frac{x_1}{x_3}} - x_1 \left(\int_{1}^{0}\frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2} dx_2 \right)_{x_3=0} - x_3 \left(\int_{1}^{0}\frac{\bar{G_2}}{(1 - x_2)^2} dx_2 \right)_{x_1=0}</math>
